As it stands you operate under the binary voting system which allows only for a carrot and stick, but no context for why either action has been taken. Split the votes.

Votes  
Interesting (blue) New (orange) Informative (yellow) Engaging (red) Funny (green)
Boring (orange-red) Repost (turquoise) Wrong {violet) Off Topic (cyan) Puerile (pink)

Then give us two votes. This way a new thread can be Interesting, but Off Topic. It can be Engaging content, but a Repost. Or it can be an Engaging piece of New content.

This breaks the binary.

Give people the ability to browse by what is Hottest by each of the 10 qualifiers, the hottest of the Puerile should sure be interesting.

Now, you will note I threw colours next to them, since we cannot have all up and down votes be the same colour. I tried throwing opposing colours against each other. Note that the only pairing I am absolutely in love with is blue for interesting and orange red for boring. Sentimental reasons for that obviously.

If making this split there is another important step to improving voting - oversight.

First review is controversy - by being the guy who flags something Repost in a dog-pile of News, you look suspicious, this puts the vote in question on a moderator page for them to check this will require that they not see the user's name or their own vote on the item of course. Basically have them see a page with the original post, and the comments that user has made in the body below - but again, without the names. This gives the Moderator a chance to tag a user as a potential troll or a contributor if they went on to prove the post was in fact a Repost.

The potential troll and contributor tags on user accounts would only be seen by moderators while they are browsing their own subreddits and would allow contributors to skip the spam folder if the moderator of the group trusts users so-tagged.

The second level of review would be randomized user peer review. Every day, for a day's worth of whatever you would call voat gold, have a user go over a page of 20 randomly made votes that do not include anything they themself have voted on. They must make two votes on each thing with only the context of the original submission and any parent posts made. Again contributing to the hidden potential troll and contributor. These peer reviews have a great weight to them than the controversy by far, because the person making a comment or post could be posting unpopular opinions in a hostile place and the reviewer won't know it.

Third level of oversight is for Administrators, when a user has a strong potential troll or contributor tag, that account is scheduled for an account review. Like with a peer review, only now a set of random contextless submissions are looked at by a random user picked for Jury Duty. This is an optional thing to also get a day's worth of voat platinum or what have you. But Jury duty picks a user at random and lets them have 4 hours to act, or it passes on to someone else. This review is about the account, is it constantly calling everyone,"fucking hivemind cockfag douchenozzels?" The review done by the Juror comes back with a recommendation of, "Warning, Punishment, Clear." No specific terms for what they did wrong, just three words, if they picked either of the negative options then an Administrator will take a look.

"A lot of words fatman, but no problem yet, what is this clickbait bullshit?" I hear you asking.

The problem is this, when someone upvotes on reddit it is not saying, "this is good content that adds to the discussion." It is however saying, "liked." Users who do not have a clear context of what they are saying about a post is good will simply agree or disagree with a post and not consider its actual value.

And without the ability to both like a thing and dislike it, you end up with boring reposts that are engaging and funny on the front page every day.

Android after years of iPhone ownership

I went from an iPhone to a Galaxy. There's always a learning curve when switching operating systems. My memory of the switch is a much greater sense of freedom. It is more complicated and more prone to issues since it's less homogenized, but I'm ok with that tradeoff. My biggest annoyances are related to unremovable bloatware and a lack of root access, problems that seem pretty ubiquitous across carriers and device types.

There is freedom, which I appreciate but with freedom comes complexity. I consider myself a high end windows power users, a fairly middle of the road linux power user and have experience with dozens of operating systems.

My last android phone, the moment was easy enough to root. I stripped everything off of it and turned it into a 3g wireless router. It ran hot though, had to keep it in a sandwich baggie in a bucket of ice to keep it from overheating.

I'll probably feel better once I've customized the hell out of this thing.

I think you touched on this some with the contacts thing, but my biggest personal hurdle was getting accustomed to an environment where the OS just provides a framework rather than doing the thing you want it to do.

For example, printing was hard for me to wrap my head around with Android. You can't really "just print" like you might do ctrl+p or cmd+p on a computer. You need to open a printing application that is appropriately connected to the printer for it to print, and each manufacturer has its own app. Sure, sometimes Google Cloud Print works across a broad range of devices, but you can't necessarily rely on that. You need to open the app, find the document or whatever, and print that out using the app.

I think depending on your perspective this can lead to impressions varying from "What the fuck is this shit?" all the way to "holy crap, I can do whatever I want.", and it all depends on what you are trying to get out of it. For a long time, the biggest gulf between Android and iOS was that iOS "just works" as pejoratively or constructively as the individual reviewer wanted that to be interpreted. The fact of the matter is that both have hit the "it just works" benchmark for a while now (I'd say 4.2/4.4 was probably when Android got as mature as it ought to be for the average user). The gulf now is a matter of perspective and desire.

The casual user can get everything at home to work in either ecosystem by buying into it (e.g. [Chromecast + Google Cloud compatible printer + Chromebook + Android] vs [AppleTV + Airprint + Macbook + iOS]), but both sides have workarounds, one is just designed to have them.

I think I took the long route in getting to this, but it's kind of the price you pay for the amount of control you have in these environments. I have no idea about iOS, but you'll probably pretty frequently see in Android a prompt to use an app every time you perform a certain action/go to a certain webpage, and that's intended to reduce the running effort of using your device. On the other hand, I almost never choose a default just because I like to keep all my options open.

Sorry if that's rambley, it's just my rambling thoughts on the whole thing.

"Everyone wants to be sold," my dad used to tell me, "you just have to find the story that sells them."

From a very young age, I was told that story telling was woven into the fabric of life. I remember being at the pool as a child, trying to get other kids to play sharks and minnows and not being very successful. "Sell the story," my dad told me. He worked on my pitch and we tried again.

"Hey, do you want to maybe play sharks and minnows?" became, "Hey, do you want to do something cool? Let's try to get the biggest sharks and minnows game ever. Let's fill the deep end. No, let's get so many people we have to take over the main part of the pool."

My request for a game became a story of what could be and fifteen minutes later we had one gang asking everyone around the pool, old and young, to play, while another gang ventured into the neighborhood, still dripping, looking for people foolish enough to stay home on a day history was being made.

That's what storytelling does - it paints a possible future for people. Something nearly tangible for them to hold in their minds and work towards. Story telling doesn't just happen in front of a campfire or on public radio, good story tellers tell their tales every day.

Storytelling is the intentional ordering of facts to create an understandable narrative.

That's what storytelling is, but what's the best place to use it?

A lifetime ago, I used to DM a game of Dungeons and Dragons. As Dungeon Master, I was the primary storyteller. I was usually able to have things well-planned out and try to accommodate any contingency, depending on how the players reacted to my world. They played the main characters in the story.

The fun started when they did something I did not expect. That meant I had to think on my feet. At that point, all my careful planning was thrown out the window for the most part and now it was my turn to have to be the one to react to changing conditions.

In the intimacy of the setting, with a group of rapt listeners hoping to glean any ounce of information that they could from me, that became one of the most satisfying and rewarding storyteller experiences I have ever had.

So, in that sense I would consider that storytelling can also be an interactive collaboration between the author and the audience. I'm sure there are many other interpretations of what being a storyteller is to different people.

I would love to hear them!
